entries: A maxim is the exact and noble expression of an important and unquestionable truth. Good maxims are the germs of all excellence. When firmly impressed on the memory they nourish the will.
Joseph Joubert, Pensées of Joubert, no. 137, Of Wisdom, Virtue, and Morality (trans. Henry Attwell, 1896)
Diary
If you can fill the unforgiving minute / With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run, / Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it, / And—which is more—you’ll be a Man, my son!
Rudyard Kipling, If, the closing four lines, Rewards and Fairies (Macmillan, 1910)
Poetry
The unexamined life is not worth living.
Plato, Apology, 38a (Socrates) (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1892)
Philosophy
I am angry nearly every day of my life, Jo; but I have learned not to show it; and I still hope to learn not to feel it, though it may take me another forty years to do so.
Louisa May Alcott, Little Women, ch. VIII, Jo Meets Apollyon (Mrs March, to Jo) (Roberts Brothers, 1868)
Fiction

Corrected: the Roberts Brothers text of 1868 punctuates with semicolons after Jo and after show it, where modernised reprints set commas. The speaker is Mrs March, whom her daughters call Marmee, answering Jo after the fall through the ice.
Had Aristotle prepared victuals, he would have written more.
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Reply to Sor Filotea de la Cruz, the philosophies of the kitchen (trans. Margaret Sayers Peden, 1982)
Correspondence

Corrected: trimmed to the sentence confirmed in Peden’s translation, the lead-in clause about trivial details being unchecked. The refuter confirmed this wording in the Penguin reprint of 1997, p. 43.
It is not reason never to yield to reason!
Sophocles, Antigone, Scene 3, his speech to his father (Haimon) (trans. Dudley Fitts and Robert Fitzgerald, 1939)
Drama
Corrected: the line number is dropped. The wording and the scene hold, but the Fitts and Fitzgerald lineation was not opened, and two printings of that translation number the line differently.
Read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; nor to find talk and discourse; but to weigh and consider.
Francis Bacon, The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Of Studies (1625, modernised spelling)
Essay

Corrected: the wording is a modernised spelling text of the Essays, which is the text that was read. The 1625 quarto prints the sentence in the original spelling of its day, so the card names the modernisation rather than claiming the quarto’s own wording.
Anyone who has received from God the gift of knowledge and true eloquence has a duty not to remain silent: rather should one be happy to reveal such talents.
Marie de France, The Lais of Marie de France, Prologue, opening sentence (trans. Glyn S. Burgess and Keith Busby, 1986)
Poetry
You must find your own quiet centre of life, and write from that to the world.
Sarah Orne Jewett, Letters of Sarah Orne Jewett, to Willa Cather, 13 December 1908, p. 249 (ed. Annie Fields, 1911)
Correspondence

Corrected: the capital Y is the card’s, since the clause runs on from must not be your audience. Fields heads the letter only Sunday, 13th of December, with no year; 13 December 1908 was a Sunday and is the accepted date. The full stop marks a cut at world.
Good things, when short, are twice as good.
Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom, maxim cv, Don’t be a Bore, p. 60 (trans. Joseph Jacobs, Macmillan, 1892)
Philosophy
It’s a dangerous business, Frodo, going out of your door.
J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, ch. 3, Three is Company (Bilbo, quoted by Frodo)
Fiction

Corrected: trimmed to the sentence that stands whole. The book sets he used to say between the two sentences, so the comma before that tag becomes the terminal stop. The words are Bilbo’s, quoted by Frodo to Pippin. The film says out your door.

Let mystery have its place in you; do not be always turning up your whole soil with the ploughshare of self-examination, but leave a little fallow corner in your heart ready for any seed the winds may bring.
Henri-Frédéric Amiel, Amiel’s Journal, entry for 2 December 1851 (trans. Mrs Humphry Ward, 1888)
Diary

Corrected: the translation year is 1888, not 1885. The entry is one Mrs Humphry Ward added to the second edition. Macmillan reads ploughshare, not the American plowshare. The full stop marks a cut at a complete clause: in Amiel the sentence runs on.

Ah, Brother, man’s a strangely fashioned creature / Who seldom is content to follow Nature, / But recklessly pursues his inclination / Beyond the narrow bounds of moderation, / And often, by transgressing Reason’s laws, / Perverts a lofty aim or noble cause.
Molière, Tartuffe, Act One, scene 5 (Cléante) (trans. Richard Wilbur, 1963)
Drama
Riches are for the sake of making life comfortable, not life for the sake of amassing riches.
Saadi, The Gulistan, chapter VIII, On the Duties of Society, Maxim I, p. 205 (trans. Edward B. Eastwick, second edition, 1880)
Philosophy
The glorious masterpiece of man is to live to purpose; all other things: to reign, to lay up treasure, to build, are but little appendices and props.
Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book III, ch. 13, Of Experience (trans. Charles Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, Navarre Society, 1923)
Essay

Corrected: the wording is Hazlitt’s later revision of Cotton as printed by the Navarre Society in 1923, vol. 5, p. 317. The 1877 Reeves and Turner text reads The great and glorious masterpiece of man is to know how to live to purpose.
And I’ve grasped some solid and useful things in drawing and in painting, more firmly than you think, my dear friend. But I keep on making what I can’t do yet in order to learn to be able to do it.
Vincent van Gogh, The Letters, no. 528, to Anthon van Rappard, Nuenen, 18 August 1885 (trans. Van Gogh Museum edition, 2009)
Correspondence
In sandy soil, when deep you delve, you reach the springs below; / The more you learn, the freer streams of wisdom flow.
Tiruvalluvar, Tirukkural, chapter 40, Learning, couplet 396 (trans. G. U. Pope, 1886)
Poetry
Two things everybody’s got tuh do fuh theyselves. They got tuh go tuh God, and they got tuh find out about livin’ fuh theyselves.
Zora Neale Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God, ch. 20 (Janie Crawford, to Pheoby Watson)
Fiction
Just as iron rusts unless it is used, and water putrifies or, in cold, turns to ice, so our intellect spoils unless it is kept in use.
Leonardo da Vinci, Notebooks, no. 1177 (The Literary Works of Leonardo da Vinci, ed. J. P. Richter, trans. mainly Mrs R. C. Bell, 1883)
Diary
Corrected: the spelling putrifies is the 1883 Richter edition’s own and not a slip. Richter files the note among the Philosophical Maxims, so Philosophy would serve as well as Diary.

In order to be happy, one must have freed oneself of prejudice, one must be virtuous, healthy, have tastes and passions, and be susceptible to illusions; for we owe most of our pleasures to illusions, and unhappy is the one who has lost them.
Émilie du Châtelet, Discourse on Happiness, the great machines of happiness, p. 349 (trans. Isabelle Bour and Judith P. Zinsser, 2009)
Philosophy

Hedged: page 349 of the Chicago volume of 2009 was never opened. The wording follows the one full quotation of the sentence, in Marcy Lascano’s draft of her 2021 article, which reads prejudice in the singular; a second Lascano paper quotes the first half with prejudices.
When you starts measuring somebody, measure him right, child, measure him right. Make sure you done taken into account what hills and valleys he come through before he got to wherever he is.
Lorraine Hansberry, A Raisin in the Sun, Act III, her speech to Beneatha (Mama) (Random House, 1959)
Drama
Travellers who require that every nation should resemble their native country, had better stay at home.
Mary Wollstonecraft, Letters Written During a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark, Letter V (J. Johnson, 1796)
Correspondence

As far as the education of children is concerned I think they should be taught not the little virtues but the great ones. Not thrift but generosity and an indifference to money; not caution but courage and a contempt for danger; nor shrewdness but frankness and a love of truth; not tact but love for one’s neighbour and self-denial; not a desire for success but a desire to be and to know.
Natalia Ginzburg, The Little Virtues, title essay, 1960, opening sentences (trans. Dick Davis, 1985)
Essay
Corrected to the book’s nor shrewdness: the anthologies smooth it to not, and PN Review 44 of 1985 printed Davis with not and a differently worded first sentence.
He who reads much and travels much sees and knows a great deal.
Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part II, chapter 25 (Don Quixote) (trans. John Ormsby, 1885)
Fiction
Well, son, I’ll tell you: / Life for me ain’t been no crystal stair.
Langston Hughes, Mother to Son, opening lines, The Crisis, December 1922
Poetry
Sweet words are like hony, a little may refresh, but too much gluts the stomach.
Anne Bradstreet, Meditations Divine and Moral, meditation IX (ed. J. H. Ellis, 1867), p. 50
Philosophy

Corrected: meditation IX is confirmed on page 50 of the Ellis edition of 1867, whose spelling hony and whose comma these are. That edition prints the long s, so refresh and stomach are modernized here. Modern printings give honey and a semicolon.
Life is the art of drawing sufficient conclusions from insufficient premises.
Samuel Butler, The Note-Books of Samuel Butler, ch. I, Lord, What is Man?, Life, ix (ed. Henry Festing Jones, 1912)
Diary
No book was so bad but some good might be got out of it.
Pliny the Younger, Letters, Book III, letter 5, to Baebius Macer, quoting his uncle Pliny the Elder (trans. Melmoth, rev. Bosanquet, 1909)
Correspondence

Corrected: Pliny reports the maxim as his uncle Pliny the Elder’s, inside quotation marks, so the words are the Elder’s and the letter is the nephew’s. The capital N is the card’s, the clause standing mid sentence.
It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye.
Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, The Little Prince, ch. XXI (the fox, to the little prince) (trans. Katherine Woods, 1943)
Fiction
In truth, whatever is worth doing at all, is worth doing well; and nothing can be done well without attention.
Lord Chesterfield, Letters to His Son, Letter LXXXI, Bath, 9 October 1746, Old Style (first published 1774)
Correspondence

Corrected: the letter number is added because the maxim recurs in Letter LXXVII, from Dublin Castle, 10 March 1746, without the opening In truth, and that is the date the reference works give. In Letter LXXXI a colon follows attention.
It is not enough to know, we must also apply; it is not enough to will, we must also do.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Maxims and Reflections, Life and Character, VI, no. 324 (trans. T. Bailey Saunders, 1893)
Philosophy

unused.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts.
unused.source: Mark Twain, The Innocents Abroad, the Conclusion (American Publishing Company, 1869)
unused.note: Verified travel line held: it widens the circle rather than counselling, and Twain is unused in the year.

unused.quote: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
unused.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 5.6 (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)
unused.note: Verified. Held because Wittgenstein can appear once in a month and proposition 7 is the stronger line for a quieter month.

unused.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
unused.source: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Proverbs of Hell, plate 7 (1790)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Blake was wanted in May for the seed time proverb, and this one speaks of time passing.

unused.quote: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.
unused.source: David Hume, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, Of the Standard of Taste (ed. Miller, pp. 229 to 230)
unused.note: Corrected in re-verification. Held: Hume sets the sentence out as the sceptical case and the next paragraph restrains it, so it wants a month about seeing clearly.

unused.quote: The butterfly counts not months but moments, / and has time enough.
unused.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Fireflies, p. 15 (Macmillan, New York, 1928)
unused.note: Corrected in re-verification to a page locator. Held: a two line poem about moments, for the month of passing things.

unused.quote: And, when you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.
unused.source: Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist, Part One (Melchizedek, the king of Salem) (trans. Alan R. Clarke, 1993)
unused.note: Corrected in re-verification to Melchizedek’s own sentence. Held: counsel, but the encouragement belongs to a month about holding on.

unused.quote: The problem in public life is learning to overcome terror; the problem in married life is learning to overcome boredom.
unused.source: Gabriel García Márquez, Love in the Time of Cholera, chapter 4 (Fermina Daza) (trans. Edith Grossman, 1988)
unused.note: Corrected: the sentence is Fermina Daza’s own. Held: it is plain speech about two kinds of life rather than counsel.

unused.quote: Give me Books, fruit, French wine and fine weather and a little music out of doors, played by somebody I do not know.
unused.source: John Keats, Letters, to Fanny Keats, Winchester, 28 August 1819 (ed. Sidney Colvin, 1891), p. 285
unused.note: Verified letter. Held: a list of things to be glad of, which is a thanksgiving rather than a maxim.

unused.quote: That’s no way to treat adventures. Never say ‘no’ to adventures. Always say ‘yes’, otherwise you’ll lead a very dull life.
unused.source: Ian Fleming, Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang: The Magical Car, Adventure Number Two (Commander Caractacus Pott) (Jonathan Cape, 1964)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Commander Pott’s counsel is about saying yes to danger, which suits a month of trial.

unused.quote: Courage is found in unlikely places.
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, ch. 3, Three is Company (Gildor Inglorion)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Gildor’s line names courage, and one Tolkien a month is the rule.

unused.quote: I rebel—therefore we exist.
unused.source: Albert Camus, The Rebel, Part One, The Rebel, closing lines (trans. Anthony Bower, 1953)
unused.note: Verified closing lines of Part One. Held: rebellion in the name of everyone belongs with what is owed.

unused.quote: Man is least himself when he talks in his own person. Give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth.
unused.source: Oscar Wilde, The Critic as Artist, Part II, in Intentions, 1891 (Gilbert)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the mask line is about how truth gets said, so it wants the month of plain speech.

unused.quote: It is not enough to be industrious; so are the ants. What are you industrious about?
unused.source: Henry David Thoreau, Familiar Letters, ed. F. B. Sanborn, to Harrison Blake, Concord, 16 November 1857, p. 371 (Houghton Mifflin, 1894)
unused.note: Verified letter to Harrison Blake. Held: Thoreau asks what the industry is for, which is a question about service.

unused.quote: It’s been my experience that you can nearly always enjoy things if you make up your mind firmly that you will.
unused.source: L. M. Montgomery, Anne of Green Gables, ch. V, Anne’s History (Anne Shirley, to Marilla Cuthbert)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Anne on making up your mind to enjoy things reads as gratitude before it reads as counsel.

unused.quote: The founding of libraries was like constructing more public granaries, amassing reserves against a spiritual winter.
unused.source: Marguerite Yourcenar, Memoirs of Hadrian, Tellus Stabilita (Hadrian) (trans. Grace Frick, 1954)
unused.note: Corrected: the full stop marks a cut at a complete clause. Held: libraries as granaries is a public duty, not private counsel.

unused.quote: The most exhausting thing in life, I have discovered, is being insincere.
unused.source: Anne Morrow Lindbergh, Gift from the Sea, chapter 2, Channelled Whelk (1955)
unused.note: Hedged: Gift from the Sea was never opened and the reference readings agree on chapter 2. Held for a month about sincerity.

unused.quote: So true is it that nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so, and conversely every lot is happy if borne with equanimity.
unused.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose IV (Philosophy) (trans. H. R. James, 1897)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Philosophy tells Boethius that nothing is wretched but thinking makes it so, which is consolation under trial.

unused.quote: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
unused.source: Francis Bacon, Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Of Studies (1625)
unused.note: Verified. Held only because Bacon lands in May with Read not to contradict; one person a month.

unused.quote: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
unused.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series, Self-Reliance (James Munroe, 1841)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Trust thyself is self-reliance under pressure more than counsel from an elder.

unused.quote: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
unused.source: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, chapter II, Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion (1859)
unused.note: Verified. Held: knowing both sides is the discipline of clear seeing, which is June’s ground.

unused.quote: I do not care what case you put; let them be sea-captains, if you will.
unused.source: Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century, on the offices women may fill (ed. Arthur B. Fuller, 1855)
unused.note: Verified. Held: let them be sea-captains is an argument about what is owed to women.

unused.quote: One day as I was sitting alone in my study surrounded by books on all kinds of subjects, devoting myself to literary studies, my usual habit, my mind dwelt at length on the weighty opinions of various authors whom I had studied for a long time.
unused.source: Christine de Pizan, The Book of the City of Ladies, Part One, ch. 1, the opening sentence (trans. Earl Jeffrey Richards, 1982)
unused.note: Corrected: the whole opening sentence is restored from the Richards translation. Held: it sets a scene in a study, which suits the month of the quiet room.

unused.quote: The cause of freedom is not the cause of a race or a sect, a party or a class,—it is the cause of human kind, the very birthright of humanity.
unused.source: Anna Julia Cooper, A Voice from the South, Woman versus the Indian, pp. 120 to 121 (Aldine Printing House, 1892)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the cause of freedom is the birthright of humanity belongs with justice.

unused.quote: Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
unused.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 7, the closing line (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)
unused.note: Verified closing line of the Tractatus. Held: whereof one cannot speak is the month of silence itself.

unused.quote: Do nothing which is of no use.
unused.source: Miyamoto Musashi, A Book of Five Rings, the Ground Book, the last of the nine rules for learning the Way (trans. Victor Harris, 1974)
unused.note: Verified, medium confidence on the Harris translation. Held: do nothing which is of no use is a rule of attention.

unused.quote: If all Men are born Free, how is it that all Women are born Slaves?
unused.source: Mary Astell, Some Reflections upon Marriage, the 1706 Preface, printed as the Appendix in the fourth edition, 1730, p. 150
unused.note: Verified. Held: Astell’s question is a demand for justice, not counsel.

unused.quote: It is this, let me tell you—that the strongest man in the world is he who stands most alone.
unused.source: Henrik Ibsen, An Enemy of the People, Act V, his last speech (Dr Stockmann) (trans. R. Farquharson Sharp, 1911)
unused.note: Corrected: this is Dr Stockmann’s last speech, not the play’s closing line. Held: standing alone is courage under trial.

unused.quote: We live close together and we live far apart. We all go through the same things—it’s all just a different kind of the same thing.
unused.source: Susan Glaspell, Trifles, the one act, near the close (Mrs. Hale) (Plays, Small, Maynard and Company, 1920)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Mrs Hale on going through the same things is about the debt between neighbours.

unused.quote: In seed time learn, in harvest teach, in winter enjoy.
unused.source: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Proverbs of Hell, the first proverb, plate 7 (1790)
unused.note: Corrected the spelling: Blake engraved In seed time as two words. Held: the proverb ends in winter enjoy, which is a thanksgiving.

unused.quote: You do not have to be good.
unused.source: Mary Oliver, Wild Geese, the opening line, Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986)
unused.note: Verified opening line. Held: you do not have to be good is a door opening, which is December’s promise.

unused.quote: Although the wind / blows terribly here, / the moonlight also leaks / between the roof planks / of this ruined house.
unused.source: Izumi Shikibu, The Ink Dark Moon, the poem beginning ‘Although the wind’ (trans. Jane Hirshfield with Mariko Aratani, Vintage, 1990)
unused.note: Corrected the edition to the Vintage printing of 1990. Held: moonlight through a ruined roof is the month of stillness.

unused.quote: Living is no laughing matter: / you must live with great seriousness / like a squirrel, for example— / I mean without looking for something beyond and above living, / I mean living must be your whole occupation.
unused.source: Nâzim Hikmet, On Living, Part I, opening lines, in Poems of Nazim Hikmet (trans. Randy Blasing and Mutlu Konuk, 1994)
unused.note: Verified. Held: living with great seriousness is a charge to hold on, which is July.

unused.quote: I got out of bed / on two strong legs. / It might have been / otherwise.
unused.source: Jane Kenyon, Otherwise, lines 1 to 4, the fourth cut at its full stop, Otherwise: New and Selected Poems (Graywolf, 1996)
unused.note: Corrected the locator: the quotation stops at the poem’s own full stop inside the fourth line. Held: it might have been otherwise is gratitude and mortality together.

unused.quote: My candle burns at both ends; / It will not last the night; / But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends— / It gives a lovely light!
unused.source: Edna St. Vincent Millay, First Fig, the whole poem, A Few Figs from Thistles (Harper and Brothers, 1922)
unused.note: Corrected the edition to the Harper text of 1922. Held: a candle that will not last the night is impermanence.

unused.quote: Now I become myself.
unused.source: May Sarton, Now I Become Myself, line 1, first sentence only, Collected Poems 1930 to 1993 (W. W. Norton, 1993)
unused.note: Corrected the locator and the edition, both at medium confidence. Held: now I become myself is a beginning, so December.

unused.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
unused.source: Italo Calvino, Why Read the Classics?, definition 6 (trans. Patrick Creagh, 1986)
unused.note: Verified. Held again: a book that has never finished saying what it has to say is the promise December keeps.

unused.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
unused.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book I, ch. 1, 980a21 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
unused.note: Verified opening of the Metaphysics. Held: all men by nature desire to know is the appetite for truth.

unused.quote: The good life is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge.
unused.source: Bertrand Russell, What I Believe, chapter II, The Good Life (E. P. Dutton, 1925), p. 20
unused.note: Verified in the Dutton text of 1925. Held: the good life inspired by love and guided by knowledge is a public creed.

unused.quote: The maturity of man—that means, to have reacquired the seriousness that one had as a child at play.
unused.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, chapter IV, Apophthegms and Interludes, section 94 (trans. Helen Zimmern, 1907)
unused.note: Corrected: Zimmern’s translation is 1907. Held: the seriousness of a child at play is a renewal, and Nietzsche stands at two of three.

unused.quote: I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it. Maybe if you found out how to live in it you learned from that what it was all about.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book II, chapter 14 (Jake Barnes) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926)
unused.note: Verified in the Scribner text of 1926. Held: Jake wants to know how to live in it, which is a search for clarity.

unused.quote: I can resist everything except temptation.
unused.source: Oscar Wilde, Lady Windermere’s Fan, First Act (Lord Darlington)
unused.note: Verified, First Act. Held: the inversion is wit about self-knowledge and the play rebukes it in the next line.

unused.quote: But then I have always supposed it to be my own fault—because I would not take the trouble of practising.
unused.source: Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice, ch. 31: vol. II, ch. 8 in the 1813 edition (Elizabeth Bennet, to Mr Darcy)
unused.note: Verified against the first edition of 1813. Held: Elizabeth on not taking the trouble of practising is a rueful thanks for what she did not do.

unused.quote: Refrain tonight, / And that shall lend a kind of easiness / To the next abstinence, the next more easy; / For use almost can change the stamp of nature.
unused.source: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 3, scene 4, lines 186 to 189, Folger edition (Hamlet)
unused.note: Verified in the Folger text. NOT AVAILABLE: Shakespeare stands at three of three for the year and cannot land again, so this line is dead whatever month wants it.

unused.quote: I often say, when I make these little observations, ‘Had Aristotle cooked, he would have written a great deal more.’
unused.source: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, The Answer, on the philosophies of the kitchen, p. 75 (trans. Electa Arenal and Amanda Powell, 1994)
unused.note: Hedged Arenal and Powell wording of the same Sor Juana sentence. Out for the year: the Peden rendering of it landed on 5 May, and the line cannot ship twice.

unused.quote: A little madness in the Spring / Is wholesome even for the King, / But God be with the Clown, / Who ponders this tremendous scene— / This whole experiment of green, / As if it were his own!
unused.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘A little madness in the Spring’, The Single Hound, poem XXXVIII (Little, Brown, 1914)
unused.note: Corrected: the poem is number XXXVIII in The Single Hound. Held: a little madness in the Spring is renewal, and Dickinson stands at two of three.

unused.quote: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway, the opening sentence (1925)
unused.note: Verified opening line. Held: Mrs Dalloway buying the flowers herself is plain speech about a whole life, and it offers no counsel.

unused.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
unused.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
unused.note: Corrected: the sentence is in The Return, Part II. Held: it is the traveller only that is foreign is a correction of the eye, which is June.

report.thinnestLane: poetry-drama: Drama at 3 of 31, the fewest of the seven tags used
